abstract: Mobility hubs are an emerging approach that often involves colocating shared bikes, scooters, cars and/or other services with transit. Together these might to provide an attractive alternative to car ownership, or otherwise support more sustainable travel behaviours. A range of signage, information displays and branding appproaches have already been developed by practitioners, but best practices are unclear.  As well, tools to help practitioners, tactical urbanists or others define their own mobility hub out of existing co-located services appear to be lacking. This paper reports the development basic tools for creating maps and a informational poster, totem or other display for mobility hubs in any location. Are there multiple mobility offerings in close proximity in your community? These tools, a printer and somewhere hang a poster might be all that is needed to spread the word.

# Introduction
Mobility hubs might help in
shifting towards more 
walking, cycling and transit-based travel 
through providing
options for those, 
more occasional, 
trips that are otherwise difficult without a car. 
They often involve implementing facilities 
for shared cars, bikes and other micro-mobility vehicles 
in close proximity to transit 
and/or with 
consistent branding, 
informational signs 
and other measures.  
However, 
in many locations 
shared cars and micro-mobility services, 
transit and other facilities 
such as bike parking 
are already in close proximity. 
Such offerings may already be well known to users or surrounding communities, 
but might be convertable into a ‘mobility hub’ 
with minimal signage and information. 


As yet there does not appear to be a 
consistent approach 
to mobility hub branding and informational displays.  
Various implementation agencies 
appear to have created 
signs, maps and similar elements 
independently. 
What might represent 
best practices is unclear.  
As well, the graphic design, 
mapping and similar needed 
to develop such signs 
for each site 
may limit the ability 
for practitioners 
to keep information up to date, 
or for bottom-up implementation,
trials or other low-cost mobility hub creation efforts.  

This paper reports findings from case and design-based research seeking to
develop new tools to support low-cost mobility hub implementation. The rest of
this paper is structured as follows: the next section outlines the context for this study. The research methodology is then described, followed by presentation of the results. 
These are then briefly discussed 
prior to a conclusion that 
includes identification of directions for future research.

# Research context
Shared bike, scooter 
and other micro-mobility 
systems have been widely 
introduced to transport systems 
over the last couple of decades. 
These may help 
to increase mobility and sustainability
but have not been entirely without problems.
Inappropriate parking of dockless vehicles, 
environmental and other impacts associated 
with rebalancing and battery swapping, 
the risk of fires at recharging facilities, 
safety challenges 
and other issues 
have been identified
(see for example @Meigs:2023aa, @Zhang:2022aa, @Bozzi:2021aa).  

The emerging 'mobility hub' concept 
may help towards limiting such issues 
and integrating shared mobility services 
into transport systems.  
Mobility hubs were part of "The Big Move" transport plan 
in Toronto, 
where the aim was to intensify landuse, 
facilitate modal transfers 
and otherwise develop major regional transit stations
[@Metrolinx:2008aa, @Metrolinx:2008ab, @Salsberg:2010aa, @Engel-Yan:2012aa]. 
@Roukouni:2023aa, however, describes how the research literature 
has extended on this to define 'shared mobility hubs' 
in terms of seamless integration of shared modes, 
sometimes including transit, 
and local facilities and services^[
*“A shared mobility hub is a place where different transport modes are integrated seamlessly, promoting efficient and sustainable urban mobility. Emphasis is given on shared mobility options such as bikes, scooters and cars. Connection with public transport (transit) is desirable but not necessary. The integration between mobility suppliers is important to provide a seamless, flexible connection at these transfer points. Ensuring an enjoyable experience for travelers is a crucial part of the hub concept as well, and therefore the hub should be considered not just as a transfer node but as a place where a variety of services come together, such as logistics services or restaurants”* (Roukouni et al. 2023).]. 
Shared *electric* mobility hubs, 
such as those currently being trialed in Ireland 
as part of the ROBUST project [@ROBUST:2025aa], 
may represent a further development 
through providing power connections 
for vehicle recharging to dedicated on-site parking space, 
thereby eliminating the need for rebalancing or battery swapping. 

Signage, branding, maps 
and other forms of public and user information 
at mobility hubs is likely 
to be of high importance 
for achieving the "integration" and
"seamless, flexible connection" 
when implementing mobility hubs.  
Basic signage, linemarking or similar 
would appear likely to be relatively easy 
for many practitioners to implement 
within their own institutional setting. 
What may be lacking, however, 
are tools and standarised approaches 
for mobility hub information provision 
based on current best practices 
that can be quickly and easily adapted to local contexts. 
As well, there may be a need for 
information displays to be refreshed 
if further offers are added to a mobility hub, 
or as the surrounding urban environment changes over time. 
People, solutions and tools tend to move on 
once decisions emerge from a policy-making effort^[c.f. the 'Garbage Can' Model. See @Lyles:1988aa, @Parsons:1995aa and others], 
which may lead to challenges for practitioners 
tasked with updates and maintenance.  

As well, political, public and institutional opposition 
can be challenging for implementing even small changes to urban environments.  Bottom-up and incremental approaches, 
‘pop-ups’ 
and more formal trials 
have proven to be successful and pragmatic strategies 
for building legitimacy *through* implementation [@Reynolds:2021ab]. 
However, these might rely on 
rapid prototyping, 
iterative co-design or 
other low-cost production 
of information displays and signage.  
Likewise, 
‘Movement and Place’ and ‘Complete Streets’ [@Delbosc:2018aa], 
and tactical urbanism approaches [@Lydon:2012aa; @Lydon:2015aa; @Davidson:2013aa; @Blumgart:2016ab; @Morhayim:2012aa; @Longhurst:2015aa] 
suggest way to challenge prevailing naratives about road space allocation, 
give communities greater power over (their own) urban environments, 
and demonstrate the potential of change.  
For practitioners, tactical urbanists 
and others to adopt a 'do it yourself' 
approach to mobility hub creation 
(especially when multiple services are already provided within close proximity, and a 'mobility hub' might be made with no engingeering works), 
there may the need for generalised tools 
to support mapping, 
signage creation and 
other sources of information.  
As of yet, 
there does not appear to be a clear understanding of 'best practices' 
in mobility hub signage and information provision, 
or tools to quickly and easily produce, maps, analysis and interpretations 
that would support the definition of a place as a hub 
and communication of its existing mobility and other offerings. 
The next section, therefore 
describes the case- and design-based methodology 
adopted in this study 
for the purposes of filling this gap.  




# Methodology

This research aims to improve understanding of 
'best practices' in 
in mobility hub signage and information provision, 
and to develop tools to support mobility hub implementation. 
Research questions relate to: 
*how* information is provided at and about mobility hubs? 
*how* information at and about mobility hubs might ideally be provided? 
(i.e. best practices) and 
*how* can such best practices be made generally applicable?*^[More formally, 
the (null) hypothesis tested in this study is that it is *not* possible to develop software tools for generating mobility hub information displays that reflect best practices and are generally applicable to other sites.] 

## Study design
The study designed 
adopts 
the Double Diamond design process [@UK-Design-Council:0aa]. 
@Coxon:2018aa and @Coxon:2021ab identify 
this as a suitable tool 
for design-based research seeking to 
develop solutions to mobility problems. 
The Double Diamond process involves 
iteration across four phases: 1. *Discovery*, 2. *Definition*, 3. *Development* and 4. *Delivery*. 
These phases alternate 
between divergent (1 \& 3) and convergent (2 \& 4) approaches, 
although the overall process 
is iterative 
and may involve 
multiple passes through each phase. 

Here the *Discovery* phase utilised a case research approach, 
which @Denscombe:2007aa, @Yin:2018ab and others 
identify as being especially effective
for when: theory development 
is at an early stage; 
research questions relate to 'how' or 'why'; and
when exploring phenomena within real-world contexts. 


## Participants, Material and Instruments
The authors were the only participants 
in the research reported in this paper. 
As discussed in the conclusion to this paper 
further research as part of the ROBUST project 
is expected to involve 
mobility hub users, stakeholders and others 
in testing, co-design and continued iteration. 
These, however, are beyond the scope of this paper.  

Material for the study was drawn from: 
photos taken during sites visits 
made by the lead author in the *Discovery* phase; 
and mapping, imagery and other online resources. 
Open Street Map datasets provided an input 
for the *Development* phase.  
 
Instruments included synthesis tables 
for cross-case comparisons. 
These were developed as per @Miles:1994aa. 
*Development* used the R programming language to 
replicate the informational display styles discovered 
at the leading cases (Bristol and Birmingham). 
Package development during the *Delivery* phase 
was guided by @wickham2023r. 

## Procedure and analysis
In the *Discovery* phase 
cases were selected from the larger sample available at https://www.como.org.uk/mobility-hubs/built-andplanned-hubs. 
Inclusion was somewhat constrained by logistics, 
but guided by the case research methodological literature (see @Eisenhardt:1989aa, @Stuart:2002aa, @Voss:2002aa,  @Eisenhardt:2007aa, @Denscombe:2007aa, @Barratt:2011aa, @Yin:2018ab and others). 
Selected cases included the leading examples of
the mobility hubs developed by the 
West of England Mayoral Combined Authority (WEMCA, Bristol) 
and Transport for West Midlands (Birmingham). 
More representative examples from Camden Council (London) 
and the London Borough of Redbridge (Woodford and Wanstead) 
were also included to provide polar opposites for cross-case comparison. 
Within each case a small number of mobility hubs were visited 
to allow for within-case comparison^[*Redbridge*: South Woodford and High Street, Wanstead; and in *Camden*: Goldington Crescent, and Doric Way; *Bristol*: Abbey Wood, UWE Frenchay, and Gainsborough Square. *Birmingham*: Huntingtree Park and Andrew Road]. 

The *Definition* phase involved synthesis of findings 
from the site visits and about each included case. 
As per @UK-Design-Council:0aa], @Coxon:2018aa and @Coxon:2021ab, 
this provided the basis for defining the problem 
that needs to be addressed by the research outputs.  

The *Development* phase involved 
iterative software coding to 
first replicate the Bristol and Birmingham 
style of information displays. 
This software was then applied to contexts of 
the ROBUST hubs in Galway, Letterkenny and Dundrum. 
Finally, a combined version that might be a step towards best practices 
was developed for the *Delivery* phase. 
This final phase involved convergence 
on a combined display style 
based on the synthesis of industry practices 
and responding to the problem developed in the *Definition* phase.  
As per @UK-Design-Council:0aa], @Coxon:2018aa and @Coxon:2021ab, 
the research also included iteration 
through all four phases. 
These iterations were tracked using the Git version control system^[Code used in the production of this paper is available at 
[https://github.com/James-Reynolds/WP5_mobilityHubTools_papers/blob/main/ReynoldsEtAl2026_CERC.Rmd](https://github.com/James-Reynolds/WP5_mobilityHubTools_papers/blob/main/ReynoldsEtAl2026_CERC.Rmd), which includes the *Delivered* software functions at the time of final submission. 
The software package itself is available at 
[https://github.com/James-Reynolds/mobilityHubTools](https://github.com/James-Reynolds/mobilityHubTools), but is expected to be developed further, so may change in the future. The last commit at the time of final submission is [a4fbbbe
](https://github.com/James-Reynolds/mobilityHubTools/commit/a4fbbbe21c5eb63640f3e9d3cc5b548237c14b19), dated August 6 2026.]. 
However, in the interests of clarity 
the next section presents 
the results in a linear format, 
stepping through each phase in turn. 


# Results
## Discovery

Table \ref{tab:synthesis_table} summarises findings from the case research^[Table notes: 1. Case study questions (column 1) are of the form 'How are details related to <COLUMN 1> at the hub communicated?' 2. An 'X' denotes an explicit mention of the feature in hub information. 'N' denotes no explicit mention, and a blank cell indicates the feature is not present at the hub. 'S' denotes secure bicycle parking, such as a locker. 3. Totem denotes a free standing information pedestal. 4. The totem / pedestal information display at the Doric Way mobility hub is specific to the Transport For London 'Cycles' docked bike share facility. There is no information provided specifically about the mobility hub.]. Figures \ref{fig:selected_images} and \ref{fig:bristol_images_panels} show selected images from various hubs.

Information displays varied between the small placard signs in South Woodford and Wanstead (Redbridge, London) to the comprehensive totems / pedestals in Bristol and Birmingham. Mobility hubs in Camden lacked any information displays, although there was a nearby totem for the bike share docking system at Doric Way (Figure \ref{fig:selected_images}, top left.). The sites themselves were labelled as "Mobility Hub" and "Local Travel Point" in Birmingham, but lacked any form of naming in Camden while the Bristol sites only showed the name of the locality (Figure \ref{fig:bristol_images_panels}). 

Totems all included two maps: one at a local scale (within 5 minutes walk) and the second showing a large area (within 15 minutes). Hub facilities were typically explictly listed or described on the totems, but not included in mapping. Linemarking was commonly used to highlight some hub components. The Bristol hubs included cube shaped indicators mounted on poles above hub components (see Figure \ref{fig:bristol_images_panels}, bottom right). 

Where present, nearby transit services and facilities where typically detailed on the information displays although this was not always the case. Insecure bike parking (i.e. locking hoops) was the most commonly provided feature, although some hubs in Camden, Bristol and Birmingham also included bicycle lockers or other limited-access facilities. Seating and nearby toilets were available as part of some hubs, but no hubs included comprehensive shelter or access to water.  The Bristol hubs included USB connections for phone recharging, and wifi internet connectivity at some locations.

## Definition

Findings during the *Discovery* phase suggest that current practices relating to information displays at mobility hubs are inconsistent. The *totems* in Birmingham, Birmingham and Doric Way perhaps demonstrate advantages of having maps and hub details displayed in large size.  The small placard signs and the lack information at most hubs in Camden provide contrasting examples where it may be unclear what facilities are provided at the hubs or nearby. 

The South Woodford placard (Figure \ref{fig:selected_images}, bottom left) provides an example of *limited information about what is provided* or *where it is* in relation to the hub. Only left or right direction indications are provided to nearby transit, taxis and shared cars. However, finding hub elements does not necessarily appear easy when maps are included on totems. Both the Bristol and Birmingham style of maps were at too large a scale for the precise location of all of the various hub offerings to be shown.  

At some hubs space that had originally been allocated to shared micro-mobility had been taken over for other purposes. Changes to the facilities and nearby services over time also meant that the original hub information displays were out of date at some sites. Consistency and the need to update information displays to reflect changing circumstances would therefore appear to be challenges facing mobility hub implementers and maintainers.    

Therefore, overall the problem to be addressed in this design-based research is to develop tools that might allow practitioners to: 1) produce totem or poster-sized information displays; 2) that clearly show hubs, surrounding facilities and services, and their location; and 3) that can be generated rapidly, cheaply and otherwise updated over time to reflect changing circumstances. Table \ref{tab:definition_details} shows five areas mobility hub information displays need to address, which have be identified based on the cases examined in the *Discovery* phase. 

```{r definition_details, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE,  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

tibble(Question = c("1. What is this?", 
                    "2. Where is it?", 
                    "3. What is here?", 
                    "4. What is nearby?", 
                    "5. How can you travel from here?"),
       Purpose = c("Define current location as a mobility hub", 
                   "Identify current location", 
                   "Identify hub elements", 
                   "Identify nearby services/facilities", 
                   "Identify spatial network context"), 
       Redbridge = c("Mobility or village hub, or 'Public Space'", 
                     "Place name", 
                     "Limited", 
                     "Limited", 
                     "Not answered"), 
       Camden = c("Not answered", 
                  "Not answered", 
                  "Not answered", 
                  "Not answered", 
                  "Not answered"), 
       WEMCA = c("Not explictly answered", 
                 "Place name", 
                 "Icons, cube markers, description", 
                 "Local and regional maps, description, direction arrows", 
                 "Description of bus/bike, bike routes on area map"), 
       TWM = c("Local Travel Point", 
               "Place name", 
               "Icons, description", 
               "Local and regional maps, description, direction arrows", 
               "Description of bus routes only")) %>% 
  kable(align = "lllll",
    caption = "Defining the design problems. Authors' concept.", 
    col.names = c("Question", "Purpose", "Redbridge London", "Camden London", "WEMCA Bristol", "TWM Birmingham"))  %>% 
  kable_styling(font_size = 7) %>% 
  column_spec(1, width = "2.25cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "2.8cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "2.8cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(4, width = "1.75cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(5, width = "2.75cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(6, width = "2.75cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  add_header_above(c("Problem" = 2, 
                     "Answers from cases" = 4)) 

```

The first question shown in Table \ref{tab:definition_details} relates to identifying a mobility hub as something in and of itself. Various terms were used in practice (Village Hub, Public Space, Local Travel Point), except in Camden (no information display) and Bristol (place name only). For the second question, the only descriptions of location are provided by place names (Redbridge, Bristol and Birmingham), while for the third question industry practices appear to be identify hub elements through text descriptions, icons and (in Bristol) the cube markers. Notably, hub elements were not always shown on maps (question 4), although both the Bristol and Birmingham information displays included these at two scales (local and larger area). Answers to the final question shown in Table \ref{tab:definition_details}(how can you travel from here?) were similarly limited, with information displays in Bristol and Birmingham in walking, cycling and bus route descriptions, while the nearby bike routes were also shown in Bristol.  





## Development


```{r download_osm_data_function, eval=FALSE, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE }

download_osm_data_by_category_function <- function(
    hub_location = hub_location, crs_local_metres = crs_local_metres, 
    key = key)
{
### Create hub locations
hub_location <- lapply(hub_location, function(x) x %>% 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), 
           crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = crs_local_metres) %>% 
  st_cast("POINT"))

place_sf <- lapply(hub_location, function(x) x %>% 
                    st_buffer(dist = 2000) %>%
                    st_transform(crs = 4326) 
                  )

placebb <- lapply(hub_location, function(x) x %>% 
                    st_buffer(dist = 2000) %>%
                    st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
                    st_bbox()
                  )
### based on https://github.com/ropensci/osmdata/blob/main/vignettes/query-split.Rmd

split_bbox <- function (bbox, grid = 2, eps = 0.05) {
    xmin <- bbox ["x", "min"]
    ymin <- bbox ["y", "min"]
    dx <- (bbox ["x", "max"] - bbox ["x", "min"]) / grid
    dy <- (bbox ["y", "max"] - bbox ["y", "min"]) / grid

    bboxl <- list ()

    for (i in 1:grid) {
        for (j in 1:grid) {
            b <- matrix (c (
                xmin + ((i - 1 - eps) * dx),
                ymin + ((j - 1 - eps) * dy),
                xmin + ((i + eps) * dx),
                ymin + ((j + eps) * dy)
            ),
            nrow = 2,
            dimnames = dimnames (bbox)
            )

            bboxl <- append (bboxl, list (b))
        }
    }
    bboxl
}

final <- list()

for(i in seq_along(place_sf)){

bb_vector <- place_sf[[i]] %>% st_bbox() %>% as.numeric()
bb <- data.frame(min = bb_vector[1:2], max = bb_vector[3:4])
rownames(bb) <- c("x", "y")               
                 
queue <- split_bbox (bb)
result <- list ()

while (length (queue) > 0) {

    print (queue [[1]])

    opres <- NULL
    opres <- try ({
        opq (bbox = queue [[1]], timeout = 25) |>
            add_osm_feature (key = key) |>
            osmdata_sf ()
    })

    if (class (opres) [1] != "try-error") {
        result <- append (result, list (opres))
        queue <- queue [-1]
    } else {
        bboxnew <- split_bbox (queue [[1]])
        queue <- append (bboxnew, queue [-1])
    }
}
final[[i]] <- do.call (c, result)
}

names(final) <- names(place_sf)

return(final)
}


process_osm_list_function <- function(
    list_to_load_and_process, 
    list_to_save_to,
    crs_local_metres){

holding <- list.load(list_to_load_and_process)
holding <- lapply(holding, function(x) 
  bind_rows(x$osm_points, x$osm_lines, x$osm_polygons, x$osm_multilines, x$osm_multipolygons) %>% 
  st_transform(crs = crs_local_metres)) %>% 
  list.save(list_to_save_to)
}
```

The *Development* phase started with creation of software tools to download Open Street Maps data and use it to replicate the Bristol and Birmingham totems, as shown in Figure \ref{fig:bristol_and_birmingham_output}. Each style includes user-adjustable hub names, facility icons and directional indicators at the top.  Maps is generated for each hub at the local and regional scales, indicating the location of nearby transit stops and stations, and highlighting buildings and other features (see detail, Figure \ref{fig:bristol_and_birmingham_output} bottom left). Icon and feature locations are generated directly from the OSM datasets, although the user can select which are to be highlighted and labeled. Finally, space is allocated for facility description text and logos.

Further *Development* involved creation of a *synthesis* display format, which responds to the problem *Definition* by: 1) adopting an A0 paper size, so as to fit with typical plotter availability; 2) leveraging Open Street Maps mapping tiles for nearby features, transit and ; and 3) explictly answering the five questions identified in the design problem *Definition* phase.  Figure \ref{fig:synthesis_poster} shows an example of the synthesis totem design generated for the Greensborough Square (Bristol).  ALSO INCLUDE AN EXAMPLE FOR ROBUST GALWAY?

The synthesis totem design has eleven elements. These in turn: answer the five design problem questions at large size that might be visible at distance (elements 1 to 5, counting top to bottom); answer the five questions again in detail and at small scale, for when standing close to the totem (elements 6 to 10); and space in the bottom right for branding or agency logos (element 11). Element 1 explicitly calls the facility a "Mobility Hub / Local Travel Point", while Element 2 includes the specific place name and details of the address, including the postal code, such that a user might be able to tell someone else (e.g. on the phone) where they are. This and further details are also shown in Element 6.   

Element 5 includes a large scale map, using the "Transport Map" tiles used by Open Street Maps from @Allan:0aa, but with additional.  



1. What is this --- MOBILTY HUB / LOCAL TRAVEL POINT / SHARED TRANSPORT STATION
2. Where is this --- NAME, 3 WORDS. POSTAL CODE. STREET ADDRESS
3. What is here and where is it --- MAP OF THE HUB FACILITIES
4. What is nearby and how can you get there --- REGIONAL MAP
5. How else can you get around --- BIKE ROUTES, TRANSIT MAP

Locating yourself: INCLUDE WHAT 3 WORDS. POSTAL CODE. STREET ADDRESS
Locating the hub facilities: 
Undertanding the surroundings ----- people have mobile phones now ---do we really need a regional map?
TRANSIT MAP









## Delivery

BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FUNCTIONS

As discussed above, this paper is part of a larger program of research seeking to develop tools for practitioners and mobility hub implementers. A developmental version is available as an R package at [https://github.com/James-Reynolds/mobilityHubTools](https://github.com/James-Reynolds/mobilityHubTools). This is a non-static version, which is expected to continue to be modified as the program of research progresses.  


APPLICATION TO THE GALWAY ROBUST HUB


# Discussion and conclusions

This design-based research has developed basic software tools that might be used in
the context of mobility hubs. The general format and styling is largely based on
elements in place at various mobility hubs in Bristol, but as discussed above the
flexibility of R might allow users to adjust layouts, styling and other details as desired.
As well as being freely available, the OSM online platform allows this dataset to be
edited by anyone, including for the purposes of mobility hub implementation
Clearly, there are many avenues for further research, including: expansion to produce
websites, posters, banners, leaflets and other informational products; developing
more generic materials for other purposes such as maintenance schedules, inspection
logs, management resources and other items that might help a mobility hub ‘product
owner’ facilitate operations, continuance and growth. Further development of ‘best
practices’ in mobility hub informational provision might involve additional case studies,
especially of non-UK sites, as well as improvements to the base ‘hub signage mockup’
developed here. There may be a need to better understand what facilities and services
might best be included as ‘part’ of a hub, as opposed to those that are mapped as
being ‘nearby’. More immediately, user testing and further development of the
software, and of the software outputs, especially the maps, would seem an important
direction for further research efforts in the short term.
This paper’s title asked a question related to the applicability of tactical urbanist
approaches to the topic of mobility hubs. Underlying this may be larger questions
related to ‘what is a mobility hub’ and ‘who gets to define and advertise something as
being a mobility hub’. Perhaps every railway station, bus or tram stop, shared or micro-
mobility facilities or many other places are already mobility hubs, but just no one has
put up a sign or handed out a leaflet that designates this as being the case? With
access to this software and a printer, turning the existing mobility offerings in your
own community into a defined hub may be within easier reach.
